newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Telstra debate slips into irrelevancy.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Telstra debate slips into irrelevancy.

text.p: Telstra's big profit has brought the government face-to-face with an intractable problem: economic policy can be impossible to explain and is highly vulnerable to politics.
The Telstra debate, already miles from the underlying logic of privatisation, has slipped further into irrelevancy in the past few days.

As soon as Telstra announced a larger-than-expected annual net profit of A$2.3 billion, non-government parties were saying the government now had the money it needed to pay for the environment package.
So it did not need to sell Telstra, they added.
This is populist politics. The connection between Telstra's profits and the environment makes no economic sense.
Reality is too hard to explain, though, and the government is trying to duck the issue by saying the budget is full of pluses and minuses.
A bit of extra cash now does not mean that the budget will still be ahead of forecast at the end of the year.

(Incidentally, Treasurer Peter Costello pointedly failed to acknowledge the unexpected tax that the government will now get from Telstra. He only admitted to the unexpected A$70 million in dividends, which Canberra Watch on Friday estimated at about A$100 million.)
But that is not really the point. If the government did have extra cash, from whatever source, it should spend it on any justifiable programmes or, more likely, use it to retire debt.
Where the money comes from should have no bearing on how it is spent.

Second, the only genuine reason to partially privatise Telstra is to remove the dead hand of public ownership from its management. Economic theory, and some practice, tells us that the company should be more efficient if private owners supervise its management.
The latest profits, big or small, make no difference to this.
But try explaining that to the voting public.
The underlying problem in all of this is a nonsense called hypothecation: attaching particular sources of revenue to particular spending purposes.
There is no point to hypothecation except in user-pays (revenue from the users, in proportion to usage), but it is irresistably attractive to voters and to the Australian Democrats.
The government got itself into this mess by promising to attach Telstra sale money to protecting potoroos, or something.
There is of course no reason why the two should be connected. If the further environmental funding is justified then the government should allocate funds from whatever source.
HARRADINE DARK ON JOB CUTS
Key Independent Brian Harradine, whose vote is needed for the Telstra privatisation, made an ominous remark on Monday that gives little comfort for the government.
Asked about Telstra's projected job cuts, he said: "Well I'm not happy."
"And that is a matter, of course, relevant to the Telstra sale legislation," he said.
"My goodness, if they can do that now, what might they do if they're privatised?"
The odds of the Telstra (Dilution of Public Ownership) Bill surviving the Senate, which Canberra Watch thought were quite good two weeks ago, are lengthening.
